CONCLUSION

The purpose of the study was to investigate the development of L2 automaticity at

the sentence level and to validate the use of CV as a measure of L2 automatization

in sentence processing. The study was a partial conceptual replication of Hulstijn

et al. (2009), using the same analyses on a subset of the same speeded tasks.
Compared to Hulstijn et al., however, the current study made important changes to

the data collection and data analysis procedures: (a) participants’ L1 background

was restricted to Korean, which is typologically distinct from English; (b) learners’

English proﬁciency was assessed independently via an online English diagnostic

test; (c) participants were likely more advanced than the high school students

in Hulstijn et al.; and (d) the sentence stimuli in the speeded tasks were made

shorter.
As a result, the CV in the sentence-related tasks did decrease as learners’

proﬁciency level increased, suggesting that the different ESL groups in this study

differed in the automatization of their L2 processing skills. This result was found

regardless of whether the data were cleaned; it lends support to Segalowitz and

Segalowitz’ (1993) hypothesis. Hence, the data from the Korean college-level

ESL students seem to justify the expansion of the CV measure to the sentence

processing level.
However, whether a smaller CV really indicates increased automaticity is still an

open question. The assumptions on which Segalowitz and Segalowitz’ (1993) logic

is based require further theoretical elaboration and empirical support; in particular,

the jury is still out on whether the elimination of initially slow subcomponents

really causes a disproportionate reduction in standard deviation and whether the

argument also goes the other way. By the same token, it seems to be difﬁcult to

Lim & Godfroid: Automatization In L2 sentence processing

falsify Segalowitz and Segalowitz’ hypothesis. If CV did not decrease, it is taken

to indicate mere speedup, whereas if CV decreased, it is a sign of automatization.

As the theoretical foundation for CV (a smaller CV means a higher level of auto-

maticity) becomes a reason for data interpretation, the argument for the validity

of CV appears to be somewhat circular. In addition to crunching numbers, we will
need psycholinguists’ insights into how L2 learners process linguistic information,

what cognitive subcomponents can be actually removed through practice, and what

aspects of L2 processing can or cannot be automatized. Although CV experiments

are far from solving the automaticity puzzle, they certainly provide interesting

behavioral pieces that will keep psycholinguists busy for some time to come.

final_decision.reason: Because the study is a digital re-analysis of the same 11 Racine plays examined by Spitzer (1931 [1928]) before expanding to a comparative corpus, its study type is reproduction, requiring the two-part reproduction outcome schema rather than a single replication outcome string. Spitzer's original study was qualitative and non-digital, so exact computational reproduction of original numerical outputs was not checked. In the first phase re-analyzing the original 11 Racine plays via formal CQP queries in TXM on annotated texts, 24 of the roughly 50 stylistic patterns identified by Spitzer could be formally modeled (making the methodological transposition of the full 50-pattern catalog only partially feasible), and for those modeled patterns the analysis verified Spitzer's cited examples and showed that the dampening patterns are even more frequent in Racine's work than Spitzer showed (robust). The subsequent finding that these patterns occur at similar rates in contemporaries—making classical dampening a genre/period style rather than a unique authorial signature—relies on a newly introduced comparative corpus of 38 contemporary plays and does not negate the confirmation of the patterns' prevalence within Racine's plays.

Although Forsythe's (2022) original dataset and code were publicly archived on Zenodo, the replicators did not run the original dataset or code. Instead, they reconstructed the 1994-2014 CPS dataset from scratch via IPUMS-CPS using modified longitudinal matching criteria (stricter age/race tolerances yielding 16,208,583 regression observations vs. 16,948,516 in the original paper), IPUMS-harmonized education, industry, and occupation variables, zero-imputation for negative potential experience, and an unfiltered Table 6 sample. The authors report that their regressions replicate the original results very closely in sign, significance, and magnitude and attribute the minor numerical differences across tables to their alternative dataset construction procedure. Because the identical original dataset was never rerun and the reconstructed-sample analysis is a test of analytical robustness (which succeeded), computational reproducibility of the original numbers was not checked.
